title: The Morning Brief: Extreme weather, conflict, and disease define a turbulent global morning
dek: North America's wildfire crisis deepened as heat records shattered, a major earthquake devastated Colombia, Ukraine struck Russian territory far inland, and Congo's Ebola outbreak doubled deaths in three weeks. The morning agenda is dominated by cascading emergencies across multiple continents.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: July 2026 set the hottest month on record in the United States, and the pattern of extreme heat is driving simultaneous wildfires, floods, and tropical storms across the continent. This weather baseline is now the backdrop for all other crises unfolding.
bottom_line: A cascading set of disasters across multiple continents and domains is unfolding simultaneously: record heat is driving the largest wildfire emergency in North American memory, a major earthquake devastated Colombia, Ukraine demonstrated new strike range deep inside Russia, and Congo's Ebola outbreak is accelerating beyond response capacity. The thread connecting many is extreme weather and heat; the others reflect ongoing conflicts and disease spread. Watch for containment progress on the largest fires (Widemouth 2, Rocky Canyon, Bald Range), casualty updates from Colombia and China as rescue operations continue, whether the Ebola death toll stabilizes or continues accelerating, jury selection pace in the Shakur trial, and whether international funding reaches Congo's health workers.
body: The hottest month in American records is behind us, and the crisis it spawned is still unfolding. NOAA confirmed that July 2026 averaged 76.9 degrees, 3.3 degrees above the 20th-century average, making it not only the warmest July but the warmest month of any kind in the agency's 132 years of record-keeping. That heat has supercharged a cascade of weather disasters still in motion: more than 30,000 personnel with over 640 crews are fighting 183 new U.S. fires since Saturday and more than 100 blazes across British Columbia, with tens of thousands evacuated. The Bald Range wildfire in British Columbia alone killed at least one person and displaced over 20,000 residents, scorching more than 53 square miles and generating its own weather system and lightning. In Utah, the Widemouth 2 fire has consumed over 118,000 acres and remains the largest in the state this year. Simultaneously, Typhoon Dolphin made dual landfalls in eastern China on Sunday with winds of 150 km/h, forcing evacuation of more than one million people from Wenzhou and Taizhou in Zhejiang province, with authorities warning of torrential rains and landslide risk through Wednesday.

Meanwhile, disaster struck elsewhere with different origins. A magnitude 7.4 earthquake centered in Colombia's Chocó province killed at least 111 people and damaged over 1,500 homes, with search and rescue operations ongoing in multiple cities. In the Ukraine-Russia war, Ukrainian drone strikes on Nizhnekamsk in Russia's Tatarstan region on August 10 killed at least 13 people, including one child, and struck an oil refinery more than 1,100 kilometers from the Ukrainian border. The strike marks one of the deadliest Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory since 2022 and demonstrates Ukraine's expanding capacity for deep-penetration operations. On the domestic front, Todd Blanche was sworn in as attorney general on Monday after the Senate confirmed him by a single vote, 50-49, following a marathon overnight session. The narrow confirmation came after weeks of uncertainty over his nomination.

A separate crisis is accelerating in Congo: the Ebola outbreak has killed at least 2,011 people among 4,381 confirmed cases as of mid-August, with the death toll doubling from 1,000 in just three weeks. The Bundibugyo virus strain driving the outbreak has no approved vaccines or treatments, and health workers are striking over pay, straining response capacity further. The outbreak is already the second-largest in history, behind only the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic.

In the courts, jury selection began Monday in Las Vegas for the trial of Duane 'Keffe D' Davis, 63, charged with murder in the 1996 drive-by killing of rapper Tupac Shakur. Davis has pleaded not guilty. Jury selection could continue through much of the week, with the trial expected to last about a month. Family members of Shakur gathered at the courthouse, with his stepbrother Mopreme expressing cautious optimism that the trial would reveal the truth.

International developments also moved: Turkey's parliament voted 468-88 to approve a conditional pardon for thousands of Kurdish PKK militants, with the pardon taking effect only after verified disarmament and group dissolution. The PKK announced last year it was ending its armed campaign and staged a symbolic disarmament ceremony in Iraq.
